title: Temporal Progression of Prior Precision, Surprisal, Model Updating and Tone Adaptation in Human Auditory Cortices
authors: van Haren, J. J. G.; de Lange, F. P.; Kotz, S. A.; De Martino, F.
abstract: Auditory perception emerges from the continuous integration of incoming acoustic signals with statistical predictions, a process complemented by simpler local adaptation. Yet, how all these concurrent mechanisms unfold in time remains underexplored. Using magnetoencephalography (MEG) in participants listening to stochastic tone sequences with periodically shifting inferential statistics, we modelled the temporal, spatial, and spectral dynamics of stimulus-specific repetition suppression, surprisal, model updating, and prior precision. By concurrently tracking these computational parameters within this dynamic auditory environment, we revealed a distinct chronological hierarchy governing predictive and adaptive processing. Prior precision states - reflecting expectations - emerged earliest, followed by rapid and concurrent repetition suppression and surprisal - reflecting local acoustic attenuation and global mismatch detection. These initial dynamics culminated in subsequent, distributed model updates within fronto-parietal networks. Spectrally, these components mapped onto diverging oscillatory fingerprints, ranging from theta-alpha modulation during adaptation to beta suppression during surprisal and broad spectral dampening during precision weighting. Together, these findings demonstrate that the brain navigates uncertain auditory environments through a cascade of neural processes, where fast, local sensory gating and mismatch signals precede the hierarchical revision of internal models.

title: Structural Basis for Human Milk Oligosaccharides Recognition by Evolutionarily Dominant Norovirus Genogroup II Genotypes
authors: Pisapia, L.; Flatau, H. N.; Lin, S.; Calamandrei, R.; Cerofolini, L.; Munoz-Garcia, J. C.; Imberty, A.; Fragai, M.; Angulo, J.; Varrot, A.
abstract: Human noroviruses are a major cause of acute gastroenteritis. Human milk oligosaccharides (HMOs) contain glycan motifs similar to histo-blood group antigens and may act as soluble decoys that reduce viral attachment. However, the molecular basis of HMO recognition by the P domain of the major capsid protein VP1 of different norovirus genotypes is not fully understood. Here, we combined ligand-based and protein-based NMR experiments with X-ray crystallography to study HMO binding to the P domain of the latent GII.2, dominant GII.4 and emerging GII.17 noroviruses genotypes. Screening of 12 HMOs by STD NMR showed binding of all fucosylated HMOs to GII.4 and GII.17 and none for non-fucosylated HMOs. In contrast, GII.2 showed little or no detectable binding under the same conditions. Seven crystal structures of GII.4 or GII.17 with complexed HMOs supported fucose anchoring via five conserved residues. The remaining sugar moieties formed genotype-specific secondary interactions with an extended, shallow and solvent exposed binding surface whose shape is dictated by divergent surface loops. GII.4 recognition is mainly driven by hydrogen bonds whereas GII.17 relied more strongly on water-mediated interactions. Chemical shift perturbation from NMR titrations (CSP NMR) of GII.4 corroborated the fucose interactions and gave dissociation constants of 20-33 mM, consistent with weak and rapidly exchanging interactions.

title: PREMISE: A Quality-Aware Probabilistic Framework for High-Resolution Source Assignment in Metagenomic Sequencing
authors: Vijendran, S.; Dorman, K.; Anderson, T. K.; Eulenstein, O.
abstract: Metagenomic applications, from influenza A virus (IAV) subtype tracking to bacterial strain resolution, frequently require sub-species resolution.However, traditional $k$-mer-based methods fragment reads into short $k$-mers and discard per-base quality scores.By omitting both intra-read linkage and error information, these methods confound closely related genomic variants, thereby impeding real-time pathogen surveillance and containment.We introduce \premise (Pathogen Resolution via Expectation-Maximization In Sequencing Experiments), a probabilistic, alignment-based framework implemented in Rust for high-resolution source assignment against near-complete reference databases.\premise aligns whole reads using a bidirectional run-length FM-index and quantifies reference abundances with a quality-aware Expectation-Maximization algorithm mapped over a taxonomy.This framework applies an optional sparsity penalty to resolve ambiguous assignments, which is particularly important when sparse samples are mapped against reference databases rich in highly homologous candidate references.On ten dense CAMI II strain-madness samples, \premise achieves the highest species-level read classification F1 score ($0.992$) among eight evaluated methods, with no false-positive or missed species.At the strain level, \premise maps reads to their source genome with top precision ($0.80$ vs. at most $0.64$ for competing methods), achieves 100\% recall, and estimates abundances as accurately as the best competing tool.These results demonstrate \premise's ability to provide rigorous, uncertainty-aware source resolution across both dense and sparse metagenomes, accurately resolving targets ranging from viral subtypes to bacterial strains.\\textbf{Availability:} \url{https://github.com/sriram98v/premise} under an MIT license.\\textbf{Contact:} \href{sriramv@iastate.edu}{sriramv@iastate.edu}\\

title: Mathematical model of phenotypic plasticity predicts interconversion is a drug target for neuroblastoma.
authors: Covell, F.; Patel, M.; Wertheim, K. Y.
abstract: Neuroblastoma is a paediatric cancer arising from the sympathetic nervous system as neural crest cells, made up of noradrenergic (NOR/ADRN/N), mesenchymal like (MES/S), and intermediate (I-type/I) cell types. These cells can interconvert between types, contributing to treatment resistance and relapse. We developed a mathematical model to investigate how interconversion patterns affect the efficacy of phenotype-specific inhibitors. We used three ordinary differential equations to describe the dynamics of the three populations, including logistic growth, interconversion, and drug-induced death. Of the 64 possible interconversion patterns, five reduced the target population: two for N cells and three for S cells. N targeting patterns were more effective with higher interconversion rates, while mesenchymal targeting patterns were more effective with lower interconversion rates. Stability analysis revealed that natural tumour growth was always unstable, but during treatment, N-suppressing patterns combined with an S inhibitor gave the most consistently stable origin. Testing multi-stage and cyclic treatment schedules revealed that N-suppressing patterns with an S inhibitor, followed by an S-suppressing pattern with an N inhibitor, achieved more reliable remission. Three of the five patterns of interest correspond to reported biological plausibility, and known compounds exist to induce most of the required transitions, supporting the clinical relevance of these strategies for improving neuroblastoma treatment outcomes.

title: Auditory Evoked Potentials Differ from Controls and Correlate with Aspects of Cognition in Kabuki Syndrome and Rubinstein-Taybi Syndrome
authors: Kalinousky, A.; Bucklin, E.; Ng, R.; Meier, L.; Jiddou, H.; Fanara, P.; Ewen, J. B.; Harris, J.
abstract: Objective Kabuki syndrome (KS) and Rubinstein-Taybi syndrome (RSTS) are two disorders caused by dysfunctional components of the epigenetic machinery and both result in intellectual disability. Mouse models of both KS and RSTS have seen reversal of cognitive impairment with epigenetic treatments. However, a great need exists for biomarkers in these disorders to improve the likelihood of successful clinical trials. This study aimed to investigate cortical auditory evoked potentials (AEPs) in KS and RSTS so that it could potentially be developed into a response biomarker in the future. Methods The amplitude of the N1-P2-N2 complex was measured for passive listening to monotonal auditory stimuli in individuals with KS, with RSTS, and typically developing controls. A standardized cognitive assessment battery was performed and specific subtests were correlated with AEP values. Results Groups differed significantly in P2, N2, and P2-N2 amplitude although RSTS was consistently more different from typically developing controls than was KS. The mid- to late-phase AEP components (P2 and N2) also correlate with cognition within and across these groups particularly with language whereas earlier components N1 and P2 correlate more with measures of executive functioning. Conclusion Late-phase components of AEPs differ in KS and RSTS from each other and from controls. KS and RSTS differ from controls in P2 and N2 amplitude in the same direction and both show a positive correlation between language and P2 amplitude and a negative correlation between language and N2 amplitude. Together they also show an association with N1 and P2 amplitude and executive functioning. Significance AEPs may turn out to be a valuable response biomarker in KS and RSTS individually and together.

title: Modeling circadian rhythm splitting under chronic light and the asymmetric transition kinetics between lighting conditions
authors: Goltsev, A. V.; Mendes, J. F.
abstract: In various vertebrates, chronic light splits the single daily 24-h circadian activity bout into two 12-h behavioral components per cycle, yet the underlying mechanism remains unresolved. Here, we develop a two-lobe biophysical model of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) to understand this phenomenon. By representing the master clock as interacting ventral core and dorsal shell populations of Kuramoto-type oscillators across bilateral lobes, we suggest that chronic light changes the excitation/inhibition (E/I) balance orchestrated by GABA, which either inhibits or excites SCN neurons. Under constant darkness, excitation dominates and provides in-phase synchronization of the populations. Under chronic light, inhibition dominates, and the ipsilateral and contralateral couplings among the core and shell populations become negative. Consequently, the shells in the left and right lobes oscillate in antiphase, producing the 12-h behavioral rhythm in downstream tissues. We suggest that this E/I balance is shifted by a light-induced change in the expression of chloride cotransporters in SCN neurons. Another key novelty is the introduction of the biologically motivated dynamics of chloride cotransporter expression, which explains the sign inversion of ipsilateral and contralateral couplings under time-varying lighting conditions. The model also reproduces the effects of unilateral SCN lesions: if one lobe is abolished, the remaining intact lobe autonomously stabilizes into a single-bout circadian output with a period comparable to that of the intact system. Finally, we compare our results with experimental data and demonstrate a close agreement.

title: Robust lesion network mapping reveals symptom-specific circuits
authors: Cui, W.; Zhu, J.; Long, Y.; Wang, F.; Yin, Y.; Wang, X.; Fu, X.; Zhang, B.; Lu, Y.; Zhang, W.; Huang, J.; Li, L.; Luan, G.; Lin, Y.; Gordon, E. M.; Wang, D.; Zalesky, A.; Dosenbach, N. U. F.; Ren, J.; Liu, H.
abstract: Lesion network mapping (LNM) is a powerful tool for linking distributed brain lesions to symptom-relevant networks, but similar LNM maps across unrelated symptoms have raised concerns about its statistical validity and specificity. Here we introduce robust LNM (rLNM), a statistically principled framework that combines two complementary controls: an anatomy-preserving spatial null model to account for connectome-derived hub bias shared across symptoms, and hypothesis-driven contrasts to resolve selective specificity among related symptoms. rLNM effectively controls both false positives and negatives. Across 10 lesion datasets (384 lesions) and two task-fMRI meta-analyses (339 experiments), rLNM recovers distinct symptom-specific networks (mean r = 0.044), which show significantly reduced similarity to the connectome hub pattern (r = 0.12 vs. 0.33 in conventional LNM). In 56 patients with neurosurgical lesions, rLNM predicts postoperative language decline at the single-patient level. rLNM thus resolves these concerns and lays a unified statistical foundation for network-symptom inferenc.

title: Neural transformation from image realism to perceived realness
abstract: Humans readily perceive whether a visual stimulus depicts something that could exist in the real world, yet the neural basis of perceived realness remains unclear. Because differences between real and unreal stimuli are ultimately expressed through visual features, realness might be expected to emerge along the ventral visual stream. Contrary to this prediction, we show that perceived-realness representations emerge in higher dorsal visual areas through a transformation of image-realism-related image-feature representations in early visual and early dorsal visual areas. fMRI revealed this representational shift toward intraparietal sulcus (IPS), with IPS patterns predicting perceived realness beyond image features and decision difficulty; source-localized MEG showed that realness coding in IPS peaked later than feature coding in early visual and dorsal visual areas. Together, these findings reveal a transformation from visual features to perceived realness along the dorsal visual stream. This representation may help guide subsequent actions and interactions with the real world.

title: A Mathematical Model of Reliability-Dependent Sensory Reweighting in Quiet Standing
abstract: Human quiet standing relies on vestibular, proprioceptive, and visual information whose contributions change with sensory context. Posturography characterizes this reweighting through responses to visual and support-surface perturbations, but a compact account of how sensory reliability propagates from state estimation to postural action remains incomplete. We develop a minimal quiet-standing model in which sensory reliability is encoded by channel-specific precision parameters that weight sensory prediction errors. A one-link inverted pendulum with intrinsic ankle stiffness estimates posture by minimizing an active-inference free-energy objective and selects ankle torque by minimizing the same objective under a restorative sensory goal. A fixed-point analysis predicts in closed form the perturbation-induced belief bias, each channel's state-update contribution, the steady posture, and a linear stability condition from the precisions, goal dynamics, and intrinsic stiffness. Closed-loop simulations in 115 trials matched the predicted equilibria to within 0.001degrees wherever the loop settled, and the two conditions predicted unstable diverged or drifted. Reducing an unreliable channel's precision eightfold reduced perturbation-driven posture shifts by 82%, with a matching decrease in that channel's state-update contribution; intrinsic stiffness left this reduction essentially unchanged for visual and sensory-only perturbations but bounded it for physical support tilts; a global precision reduction did not reduce the shift; and a within-trial precision switch showed belief updating, not a separate action gain, carrying the change to ankle torque. The results give a compact mathematical account of postural sensory reweighting as relative, context-selective precision control in a closed multisensory loop.

title: Emergent topological structure in spontaneous brain-organoid activity
authors: Bodnia, E.; Basart, M.; Hai, S.; Ford, L.; Miolane, N.; Kosik, K. S.; Bouwmeester, D.; Carr, L. D.
abstract: Neural activity is widely held to organize on low-dimensional structure embedded in a high-dimensional state space. Persistent homology reads such structure directly from the pattern of pairwise correlations, without assuming in advance which variables are relevant. We apply persistent homology to microelectrode-array (MEA) recordings of spontaneous activity from human (Lancaster) and mouse (Pasca) cortical organoids, spanning 25-197 sorted units, and ask whether topological data analysis resolves structure at the node counts that neural recordings actually deliver. Building weighted networks in correlation space and characterizing them by Vietoris-Rips filtration, we find that the first homology (H1, loops) rises significantly above a rate- and population-preserving null in 14 of 18 datasets, all of which remain significant after correction for testing 18 datasets. Random removal of neural units leaves the loops largely intact. Removing the units that form the loops disrupts them more than removing equally connected units does. Topological richness grows with network size, and second homology (H2) exceeds the null only in the larger networks. These results show that persistent homology resolves structured topology in neural recordings at the scale experiments actually deliver.

title: Dual regulation of chemical stress-induced DDI2/3 expression by a transcription factor Fzf1 and nucleosome in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
authors: Du, Y.; Lin, A.; Brown, J. A. R.; Howe, L.; Xao, W.
abstract: DDI2 and DDI3 (DDI2/3) are duplicated genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae that exhibit strong induction by a transcription factor Fzf1 in response to chemical treatments like cyanamide (CY) and methyl methanesulfonate (MMS). Although, like DDI2/3, SSU1, YHB1 and YNR064C also contain an Fzf1-binding consensus sequence CS2 and are coordinately regulated by Fzf1, these genes are only modestly induced by CY and MMS. To identify additional cis-acting elements in the DDI2/3 promoter, we made DDI2/3 promoter deletions in a reporter system and identified upstream repressing sequences (URS) spanning 480 nucleotides. To test a hypothesis that the chromatin structure constitutes the URS, we utilized a yeast strain capable of histone H3/H4 depletion by shifting carbon sources. Following histone depletion, DDI2/3 were strongly induced in an Fzf1 dependent manner, while YHB1 was repressed. Interestingly, under histone depletion conditions, CY or MMS treatment further increased expression of all Fzf1-regulated genes to comparable levels in an Fzf1 dependent manner. A genome-wide MNase-seq analysis showed that CY treatment reduced the nucleosome occupancy at the mapped DDI2/3 URS region in wild-type cells, but not in in fzf1{Delta} cells. These findings collectively indicate that Fzf1 plays dual roles in regulating the DDI2/3 response to CY. Firstly, it binds CS2 and serves as a transcription activator. Secondly, it is required for the chromatin remodeling at URS. This two-tier regulation at the DDI2/3 promoter helps to explain why DDI2/3 achieve much higher fold induction by CY and MMS than other Fzf1-regulated genes, suggesting Fzf1 to be a candidate pioneer transcription factor.

title: ER stress-associated IRE1α signalling links impaired QPRT-dependent NAD⁺ biosynthesis to reduced oocyte competence
authors: Athar, M.; E, A. K.; Birajdar, P.; M, R.; Kumar, A.; Kumari, A.; Sabnam, S.; Verma, A.; L, P.; Nial, P. S.; G, T. S.; Prasada Rao, H.
abstract: Oocyte quality is closely linked to metabolic and organelle homeostasis, but the mechanisms underlying naturally occurring differences in oocyte quality remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify a link between endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress, impaired NAD biosynthesis and poor oocyte quality. Poor-grade goat oocytes exhibited profound NAD depletion, accompanied by quinolinic acid accumulation and reduced expression of quinolinate phosphoribosyltransferase (QPRT), suggesting a bottleneck in de novo NAD biosynthesis. Restoring QPRT expression or bypassing this metabolic step improved meiotic maturation. Further analyses revealed altered ER stress signalling, increased IRE1-associated activity and reduced QPRT RNA stability. Recombinant IRE1 processed QPRT RNA in vitro, suggesting a possible link between IRE1 activity and QPRT transcript regulation. Supplementation with nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) restored NAD levels and improved several features of poor-quality oocytes, including calcium homeostasis, oxidative stress and mitochondrial membrane potential. NMN treatment also improved early embryonic development, with its beneficial effects involving SIRT6 activity and changes in DNA methylation-associated fluorescence. Importantly, NMN supplementation improved meiotic maturation in poor-grade bovine and porcine oocytes, indicating that this metabolic intervention may have broader relevance across mammals. Analysis of published human oocyte proteomic data further revealed age-associated changes in ER proteostasis and NAD-related proteins. Together, our findings identify ER stress-associated disruption of QPRT-dependent NAD biosynthesis as a potential contributor to poor oocyte quality and suggest that restoring NAD metabolism may offer a strategy to improve the functional properties of compromised oocytes.

title: A Dynamic Stem Cell State Links Environmental Cues to Skeletal and Regenerative Fates
authors: Wang, Y.; Zhao, L.; Chen, K.; Xiang, J.; Hunt, E. J.; Sokol, J.; Ding, K.; Steininger, H. M.; Martinez, N. R.; Weldon, K. C.; Chan, E.; Morales, D. A.; Martinez, C.; Wang, S.; Marquez-Arreguin, G.; Chen, H.; Hoover, M. Y.; Lu, W.-J.; Xiao, J.; Guo, F.; Longaker, M. T.; Weissman, I. L.; Chan, C. K. F.; Ambrosi, T. H.
abstract: Stem cells faithfully generate tissue architecture during development, yet how their identity and regenerative output are reshaped as anatomical niches mature and environmental signals change with aging and injury remains poorly understood. Rare skeletal stem cells (SSCs) across diverse skeletal sites are defined by combinations of cell-surface markers, precluding their genetic interrogation in vivo. Here, using spatially informed single cell transcriptomics, we identify Pannexin-3 (Panx3) to mark a dynamic functional state within bona fide SSCs and establish Panx3-CreERT2 mice for its longitudinal interrogation. Panx3 SSCs exhibit long-term clonal persistence, self-renewal and multipotency, whereas Panx3- SSCs can acquire this state. Successive SSC cohorts engage the Panx3 state during skeletal development, osteoanabolic stimulation expands pre-existing Panx3 SSC clones and injury induces it locally in previously unlabeled progenitors. Thus, anatomically distinct progenitors can converge on a common stem cell state in response to different environmental inputs. Three-dimensional reconstruction of chondrogenic niches further identifies signals that redirect Panx3-lineage cells towards stable cartilage, enabling durable regeneration in aged and osteoarthritic joints and with human SSCs. These findings establish anatomical origin, stem cell state and lineage fate as separable dimensions of stem cell identity and provide genetic access for interrogating and directing endogenous SSC function.

title: Proteome-wide profiling reveals compartment-specific RNA buffering of protein aggregation during stress
authors: Seidler, J. F.; Thelen, F.; Wäber, N. B.; Weber, J.; Lohle, L.; Timm, T.; Lochnit, G.; Blom, J.; Goesmann, A.; Strässer, K.; Kilchert, C.
abstract: Cellular adaptation to stress requires extensive remodeling of RNA metabolism. The rewiring of the RNA-protein interaction landscape and the assembly of biomolecular condensates are central to this response, yet the global stress-induced reorganization of macromolecular RNA-protein assemblies remains incompletely characterized. Here, we apply R-DeeP, a density gradient approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry, to profile the RNA-dependent sedimentation behaviour of the Saccha-romyces cerevisiae proteome during heat and salt stress. We demonstrate that stress triggers a profound, stress-specific reorganization of the RNA interactome. Many proteins undergo pronounced, selective shifts into high-molecular weight fractions, indicative of aggregation. RNase treatment markedly exacerbates this aggregation, consistent with the model that RNA acts as a general chaperone that keeps proteins with intrinsically disordered regions soluble. Strikingly, our data demonstrate that this protection is compartmentalised. Nuclear proteins are partially shielded from stress-induced aggregation. This protection coincides with the nuclear accumulation of RNA caused by a block of RNA export during stress, and RNase treatment abolishes this protection. Nuclear RNA retention may therefore act as a buffer that actively increases the local chaperoning capacity of the nucleus. In contrast, cytoplasmic proteins, including translation factors and ribonucleoprotein granule components, exhibit increased aggregation under stress. Fluorescence microscopy confirmed that increased biochemical aggregation in density gradients reflects changes in assembly state in vivo. For many stress-induced aggregators, these changes are visible as spatial reorganisation in stressed cells, such as the formation of foci. Our findings suggest that cells use subcellular RNA distribution to tune the condensation and/or aggregation threshold of proteins in a compartment-specific manner.

title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. In response, we developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Analyses reveal centromere-length differences between related lineages, extend observations of short non-centromeric arrays across a lineage, and show unequal component variability and composition changes with heterochromatin length within lineages. Yruler brings satellite variation into population-scale phenotype studies.

title: Epigenome-informed Polymer Modeling Reveals Chromosome Folding Landscapes across Distinct Genetic and Epigenetic Contexts
authors: Bazmi, S.; Turco, A.; Kumar, S.
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is critical for gene regulation, enabling long-range interactions between genes and distal regulatory elements. Genomic structural variations and epigenetic differences can perturb this organization, contributing to phenotypic variation and tissue-specific gene regulation. Prior studies have assessed the impact of these genetic and epigenetic changes on 3D genome folding, primarily using population-averaged features such as topologically associating domains and loops. However, growing evidence from single-cell and live-imaging studies indicates that chromosomes are highly dynamic and exist as heterogeneous ensembles of conformations. Here, we applied an epigenetic-state-informed polymer modeling framework to generate chromosomal conformational ensembles directly from cell- and tissue-specific epigenomic data. The resulting ensembles reproduced experimental Hi-C maps across cell lines and tissue types. Comparison of these conformational ensembles revealed that, although polymer dynamics were conserved across cell lines, their folding landscapes diverged. These differences arose primarily from cell-line-specific chromatin-state interaction networks and were concentrated in rare, long-lived contacts. Furthermore, modeling a TAD-boundary-disrupting deletion without re-optimizing the model parameters indicated a shift in the chromatin conformational ensemble from predominantly insulated to predominantly fused states. The modeled deletion also selectively strengthened active chromatin contacts and differentially disrupted enhancer contacts involving neighboring genes. Finally, comparison of two tissue types from the same donor revealed epigenetically driven rewiring of chromatin-state interaction networks. These findings establish chromosomal conformational ensembles as a sensitive readout of genome reorganization across distinct genetic and epigenetic contexts.

title: Sexing carnivores from faecal metagenomes: calibrating Rx for stone marten and red fox
authors: Vujic, V.; Mayer, C.; Helyes, G.; Maroti-Agots, A.; Maroti, G.; Csabai, I.; Solymosi, N.
abstract: Knowing the sex of the animal that deposited a scat adds value to non-invasive monitoring, but read-ratio sexing methods were developed for human ancient DNA. We examined their use in shotgun metagenomes of seven stone marten (Martes foina) and red fox (Vulpes vulpes) scats. Human DNA, present in every library, was removed by competitive mapping against the host assembly and the human reference. Applying the Skoglund Ry metric to the marten samples yielded 0 to 25 Y-mapping reads per sample and failed to identify either of the two animals that Rx places firmly in the male range, so we adopted the X-to-autosome ratio Rx of Mittnik et al. instead, reimplemented as an open-source, species-agnostic Python tool. To test whether its human-derived thresholds transfer, we simulated female and male genomes of both species and drew 200 replicate subsamples at each of fourteen depths from 1,000 to 100,000 mapped reads. Nine of 11,200 replicates were assigned to the wrong sex, all of them below 2,000 mapped reads; above that depth the only failure was non-assignment, in under 5% of replicates above 7,500 reads and under 1% above 15,000. Applied to the scats, Rx identified four females and two males; one sample with 596 host-assigned reads was left unassigned. With competitive removal of human reads, Rx and its original thresholds are usable in these carnivores.
